title: When or where?
instructions: Sort each detail: does it tell you WHEN the story happens, or WHERE?

items.text: Frost still clung to the car windows.
Between the lockers and the trophy case
Just before the last bell of the day
Up in Grandma's dusty attic
Back when horses pulled the carts through town
On the slippery steps of the harbour

title: Specific details
instructions: Tap the three details that make this classroom one specific place, not any classroom.
text: Mr. Okafor's classroom had a wobbly globe, a snake tank humming in the corner, and a clock that ran ten minutes fast.
explanation: A wobbly globe, a humming snake tank and a fast clock belong to THIS classroom. Specific details let readers picture one real place.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives the clearest setting?

options.text: It was somewhere, at some point.
On the last night of summer, the fairground lights blinked on one by one.
They went to a place.

questions.explanation: "The last night of summer" tells you when, and "the fairground" tells you where, with a detail you can see.
questions.hint: Look for a sentence that answers both when and where.

questions.prompt: Which detail shows it is early morning without saying "morning"?

options.text: The milk van rattled past as the first birds began to sing.
It was a nice day.
The moon was high and the streets were silent.

questions.explanation: The milk van and the first birdsong are clues to early morning. The moon high in the sky points to night.

questions.prompt: Why are specific details better than general ones?

options.text: They make the story longer.
They help the reader picture one real place.
They use harder words.

questions.explanation: "A red door with peeling paint" lets the reader see one door. "A door" could be any door.

title: Setting snapshot
prompt: Describe a real place you know at one specific time (your kitchen on a school morning, the bus stop in the rain, the park at sunset). Make the reader know when and where without just naming them, using details only this place has.
tips: Show the time with clues: the light, the weather, what people are doing.
Pick one detail nobody else would notice.
Use at least two senses: what do you hear and smell?

title: Calm or tense?
instructions: Sort each setting detail by the mood it builds.

items.text: Waves lapped gently against the boat.
A twig snapped somewhere behind them.
The cat dozed in a square of warm sunlight.
The door handle turned, slowly, by itself.
Grass swayed across the quiet meadow.
An alarm shrieked, then stopped dead.

title: Building a bright mood
instructions: Tap the three words that make this market feel bright and cheerful.
text: Golden lanterns swung above the stalls, oranges glowed in their crates, and the fountain sparkled in the sun.
explanation: Golden lanterns, glowing oranges and a sparkling fountain all fill the market with light. The writer never had to say "cheerful".

questions.prompt: Which detail makes a forest feel dangerous?

options.text: Birds sang in the sunny branches.
Something large crashed through the bushes, and the birds went silent.
A family had a picnic by the stream.

questions.explanation: A crash and a sudden silence warn the reader that something is wrong. That's how you build danger without naming it.
questions.hint: Which detail would make you stop and listen?

questions.prompt: Which sentences build a tense mood best?

options.text: The stairs creaked. Then silence. Then another creak, closer.
The stairs, which were made of old wood, creaked a little bit as people went up and down them during the day.
The stairs were nice.

questions.explanation: Short, sharp sentences and a sound that comes closer make the reader hold their breath.

questions.prompt: "A fire crackled in the hearth, and Grandpa tucked a blanket around my knees." What mood does this build?

options.text: Safe and cosy
Dangerous
Gloomy

questions.explanation: A warm fire, a blanket and a grandparent are all safe, familiar details.

title: Mood maker
prompt: Choose a mood on each scale. Then describe one place (a school hallway, a playground, a kitchen or a beach) so the reader feels that mood. Build it with light, weather, sounds and objects, not by naming the mood. Quill will tell you what mood a reader feels.
tips: Use the word bank for ideas, then add your own.
Tense? Try short sentences and sudden sounds. Calm? Try long, flowing ones.
Pick details that all point the same way.

moodPicker.label: Set the mood of your place

title: Explaining or showing the world?
instructions: Sort each sentence: does it explain the world's rule, or show it through everyday life?

items.text: In this world, everyone can read minds.
At dinner, Mum answered Leo's question before he asked it, so he thought about pudding instead.
The city was built underwater a long time ago.
Kids raced to school on seahorses, and the bell was a whale's low hum.
On this planet, the sun never sets.
Bedtime meant pulling on a thick eye-mask and closing the metal shutters against the afternoon glare.

title: World clues
instructions: Tap the three words that show how this world is different from ours.
text: Every morning, Juno watered the cloud in her garden, paid for bread with a song, and waved to the moon as it rolled past.
explanation: A cloud you water, bread paid for with a song, and a moon that rolls past are everyday details in a world with different rules.

questions.prompt: What makes an invented world feel believable?

options.text: A long explanation of all its rules at the start
Small, everyday details that show how people live there
Lots of made-up words on every line

questions.explanation: When characters do ordinary things in an unusual world, readers believe it, and they work out the rules themselves.
questions.hint: Think about what makes a real place feel real.

questions.prompt: In a world where it's always winter, which detail shows it best?

options.text: It was always winter there.
Nobody in the village had ever seen a flower, except in Grandma's old book.
The village was nice.

questions.explanation: Never seeing a flower is a small, surprising detail that shows the endless winter without explaining it.

questions.prompt: Which question helps you invent everyday details?

options.text: What do kids here eat for breakfast?
How long is my story?
What colour is my pen?

questions.explanation: Thinking about ordinary life (food, school, chores) gives you details that make the world feel lived in.

title: A day in my world
prompt: Invent a world where one thing works differently from ours. Describe a normal morning there, showing the rule through at least three everyday details (breakfast, getting to school, chores). Don't explain the rule: let the reader work it out.
tips: Decide your one big rule first, then ask: how would it change breakfast? School? Bedtime?
Make one detail funny or annoying. Normal problems make strange worlds feel real.
Make it clear when and where we are.

title: Helps or blocks?
instructions: Each character wants to get somewhere fast. Sort each setting detail: does it help them or block them?

items.text: The road is a sheet of black ice.
A hidden shortcut cuts through the hedge.
The market is packed shoulder to shoulder.
A strong wind pushes their boat towards the shore.
The old bridge has collapsed into the river.
A full moon lights up the path.

title: Setting in motion
instructions: Tap the three action words that show Sam moving through the setting.
text: Sam ducked under the dripping branches, splashed across the stream, and scrambled up the muddy bank.
explanation: Ducking, splashing and scrambling let you discover the woods, the stream and the bank as Sam moves through them. Setting and action at the same time!

questions.prompt: Which setting causes the biggest problem for a character trying to deliver a cake?

options.text: A sunny, empty street
A steep hill covered in fresh snow, with a dog that loves cake
A tidy kitchen

questions.explanation: A slippery hill and a hungry dog both get in the way. A setting that causes trouble creates a story.
questions.hint: Which setting makes the job hardest?

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows the setting through the character's actions?

options.text: The cave was dark and wet.
Ana felt along the slimy wall, her torch flickering, water dripping down her neck.
There was a cave.

questions.explanation: We learn about the cave (slimy, dark, dripping) from what Ana touches and feels as she moves.

questions.prompt: Why let the setting cause a problem?

options.text: It turns description into action, so the reader wants to know what happens.
So you don't need characters.
It makes the setting less important.

questions.explanation: When the setting gets in the way, the reader worries about the character, and the description becomes part of the story.

title: The setting fights back
prompt: Choose the mood of your scene. Then write a scene where a character is trying to get somewhere or do something, and the setting causes a problem (weather, a locked door, a crowd, a steep cliff). Show the place through what the character sees, hears and touches as they move.
tips: Start with what your character wants to do right now.
Let the setting make it harder at least twice.
Use at least three senses, and keep details pointing to your chosen mood.

moodPicker.label: Set the mood of your scene
